claims.text: The starting HfNbTaTiZr alloy is a single-phase bcc random solid solution or low-density-SRO state.
HfNbTaTiZr has thermal conductivity in the range of 10–17 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Lattice distortion and defects depress electron and phonon propagation and contribute to the low thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr.
Controlled annealing or rapid quenching can evolve SRO from isolated clusters into a percolating network in HfNbTaTiZr while retaining a single-phase bcc structure.
Second-phase precipitation, including Laves-phase formation, can be avoided during the proposed SRO evolution.
Between the ODTT and melting point, exemplified by 800–1500 K, SRO remains stable while HfNbTaTiZr remains single-phase bcc.
Crossing the ODTT changes or eliminates SRO and can alter precipitation behavior in refractory multicomponent alloys.
Isolated SRO clusters act as phonon-scattering centers and reduce thermal conductivity.
Percolating SRO clusters form coherent, low-scattering pathways that bypass the disordered matrix.
SRO percolation creates a connected, lower-energy potential landscape for phonon propagation.
SRO can flatten the energy landscape for edge dislocations, reduce solute drag, and enhance edge-dislocation mobility.
The edge-dislocation energy-landscape effect is analogous to, and can be extrapolated to, phonon transport through percolating SRO.
Thermal conductivity will first decrease with increasing SRO, reach a minimum at an intermediate SRO volume fraction, and then increase after SRO percolation.
The magnitude of the post-percolation conductivity increase will correlate with the percolation threshold of the SRO network.
Standard serial/parallel mixing models and simple scattering theories predict a monotonic decrease in thermal conductivity as SRO concentration increases.
The proposed conductivity increase requires coherent SRO domains that do not introduce new interfacial defects.
The proposed mechanism does not apply if SRO develops into a second phase or amorphous structure, becomes incoherent, or fails to percolate.
A sample series spanning isolated to percolating SRO, with conductivity and SRO topology measured together, can distinguish a percolative transition from a simple monotonic scattering response.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis permits or predicts decreasing conductivity below the critical percolation threshold, but the falsification rule says that a monotonic decrease up to the point of percolation is itself sufficient to falsify the hypothesis. The decisive criterion should instead be the absence of an increase after the independently identified percolation onset.
